hints.title: Greedy Cut Priority
hints.text: Each cut multiplies by the number of existing perpendicular pieces. Expensive cuts should be performed as early as possible before perpendicular pieces multiply.

hints.title: Two Pointer Traversal
hints.text: Sort both cut cost arrays in descending order. Compare the highest remaining horizontal cut with the highest remaining vertical cut.

hints.title: Piece Tracking
hints.text: Whenever a horizontal cut is chosen, multiply its cost by the current count of vertical segments and increment the horizontal segment count. Symmetrically handle vertical cuts.

hints.title: Reference Implementation
hints.text:
```python
class Solution:
    def minimumCost(self, m: int, n: int, horizontalCut: list[int], verticalCut: list[int]) -> int:
        horizontalCut.sort(reverse=True)
        verticalCut.sort(reverse=True)
        h, v = 0, 0
        h_pieces, v_pieces = 1, 1
        total_cost = 0
        while h < len(horizontalCut) and v < len(verticalCut):
            if horizontalCut[h] >= verticalCut[v]:
                total_cost += horizontalCut[h] * v_pieces
                h_pieces += 1
                h += 1
            else:
                total_cost += verticalCut[v] * h_pieces
                v_pieces += 1
                v += 1
        while h < len(horizontalCut):
            total_cost += horizontalCut[h] * v_pieces
            h += 1
        while v < len(verticalCut):
            total_cost += verticalCut[v] * h_pieces
            v += 1
        return total_cost
```

complexity.time: O(m log m + n log n)
complexity.notes: Sorting cut cost arrays dominates the linear greedy scan.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Testing all possible permutations of cuts requires exponential factorial time.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: In-place sorting keeps extra space at O(1).
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Explains why greedy cut ordering is provably optimal using piece multipliers.
